blocks.p: On Serenity the snow fell upward first.

Sol Tarren watched it from the departure concourse while Pell saw to the luggage. Somewhere out on the ice a seam had opened, and the sea beneath it breathed out: a long white plume that rose without a sound into the black, hung above the horizon as if deciding something, and came drifting back so slowly that it did not seem to be falling at all. By the time it reached the terminal it was only a fine frost on the glass. People found it restful. Sol had found it restful too, for three hundred years. He watched the frost settle now and could not find the rest in it anywhere.

His travel case stood at his feet. He had carried it from his quarters himself, which he never did, and when the porter reached for it he had said, “No, thank you,” in a voice that made the young man step back. There was nothing in it anyone would have looked at twice: his traveling vestments, two stoles, the Book of Life in its white binding with his name stamped in gold. And under all of it, wrapped in a shirt, the other two books. He had not opened them. He had only felt their weight when he lifted the case, and their weight was very slight, and he had felt it all the way down the corridor.

“Your Grace.” Pell came back across the concourse with his tablet. “We’re boarding in ten minutes. Forward cabin; you’ll have it to yourself.” He reached up without asking and set the fold of Sol’s stole straight at the shoulder, as he had every morning for sixty years, and glanced at Sol’s face, and then down at the tablet, and hesitated, which he almost never did. “You’ve seemed tired, Your Grace. These last days. If I may say so.” He found the agreeable thing, as he always found it. “It isn’t long to the autumn now.”

It was not long. In the autumn he would cross home to Sion and lie down under the hood in the east hall, in the good chair beside Aurelian’s, and wake younger, and lighter, and the old man would be gone with every other heavy thing. Perhaps he would remember a sad case on Mars. Perhaps not even that. It would take care of it, as it took care of everything.
“Thank you, Deacon,” he said, though Pell had offered him nothing but the season.

He had not believed a word of what Stephen told him in the cell. And then he had gone down to Mercy Hall and watched a girl go up into the City with a warden’s hand in hers, and it had been as gentle as the church had always said, and he had been glad; and the next morning, in the same faith, he had signed for Stephen. They aren’t going where you think. He had turned that over so many times since that it had worn smooth, like a stone carried in a pocket, and he no longer had to look at it.
And then the old man had looked at him one last time, and said what he had said. Do not hold this against him.
The plume outside had settled. The horizon was black and clean again. Sol picked up his case.

The Concord packet was a squat local hauler that made the run between the two moons twice a day. It carried no stasis pods; Europa and Ganymede were neighbors, as such things went, and no one needed freezing for a crossing of eleven hours. The forward cabin held twelve grey seats and a long port that showed the sky. A steward met them at the hatch. He was young, with the unfinished look of a first life, and a strip across his tunic said ROE.
“Your Grace.” He bowed lower than he needed to. “Remember the Mountain.”
“And forget the tears.”
“Can I bring you anything? Water? There’s real tea, from Abundance.”
“Water,” Sol said. “Thank you.”

The young man brought it in a sealed cup and went back to his station behind a half-partition at the rear of the cabin, from where, now and then, he stole a glance forward. People did that around bishops. Sol had stopped noticing it centuries ago, and he noticed it now.

They launched. The thrust pressed him into the seat and eased to a steady lean, a tenth of a weight. Out the long port the ice fell away, white and cracked like an old plate, and then it was behind them, and in its place, filling half the sky, there was Jupiter.

Sol had seen it ten thousand times. He looked at it now as though he had not: the bands of cloud, cream and rust and a brown like old blood, and the great storm low on the face of it like an eye. He found he was thinking that it would still be beautiful when every person who had ever looked at it was gone, and that it would not care, and that this was not a thought a bishop of Life was supposed to have.

Across the aisle Pell worked through the correspondence. “Bishop Croft has called twice; I told him you were traveling. The Hierarch’s office wants your report on the failures by the end of the month. I’ve drafted something.”

It opened in the corner of Sol’s sight: old relays, ice in the lines, and a last paragraph so smooth and warm that Sol heard his own voice in it. Sixty years of drafting his letters had taught Pell exactly how His Grace turned a hard thing into a kind one. It was a tidy answer in the Tarren manner, and Sol found that he wanted to sign it. He wanted the praise that would come back for it, and he was ashamed to find the wanting still in him, here, with two forbidden books in the case at his feet.

There was nothing in it about a cantor who taught for nothing, or a miner whose pay went to strangers. There was nothing about the blank field on every failed file, or a noise that rose and fell like responses behind a door, or a mother’s eyes in the City.
“Hold it,” he said.
“Your Grace?”
“Don’t send it. Not yet.”
“Of course, Your Grace.”
The pressure came back behind his left eye.

It came as it always came, a thumb pressed gently from inside, and he sat still and waited for it to go. It did not go. It pressed, and kept pressing, and then it was not a thumb anymore but a whole hand, flat and warm against the back of his eye, and he had the strange, clear thought that someone was standing directly behind him and leaning close.
He unbuckled his harness.
“Your Grace?”
“I want to see it.” He did not know what he meant. He stood. In the light thrust it was easy; he rose out of the seat as if lifted. “I want to see it properly.”
“Your Grace, the harness...”
“We’re barely under way, Deacon. I’ll hardly fall.”
He took two steps toward the port. On the second step he smelled rain.

It was not the recycled air of the cabin. It was rain on hot stone, and something green underneath it, crushed leaves, wet earth, a smell so sudden and complete that he stopped with his hand half raised toward the glass. He had not smelled rain in four hundred years. He did not know how he knew that it was rain. And with it came a feeling he had no word for, a rising, as if the floor of his stomach had come loose and was lifting up through his chest toward his throat, and the light from the port went very bright, brighter than Jupiter could make it, and the cabin seemed to lengthen away from him on every side.
Pell, he tried to say, and could not find his mouth.
Somewhere a man cried out, a high strange cry with all the air in it, and Sol thought with great calm: Someone is ill. Someone should help him.
Then the light took him.

It was not the gold light of Abundance, which made fruit glow and faces smooth. It was white, and it did not flatter anything. It lay over everything like water over stones in a clear stream, and everything it touched was exactly what it was and nothing else, and he understood that he had never in his life seen anything by a light like this one.
In it he saw himself.

He was lying in the good chair in the east hall in Sion, under the hood, with his eyes closed and his face at peace. Then there were two of him, and ten, and a hundred, lying one behind another down a long hall of white, every Renewal of four centuries laid out like the pages of a book, and he could see into each of them. He could see what was taken. It came out of him gently, in threads, the way you would draw a splinter: here a friend’s face in a room full of screens; here a long-nosed woman at the end of a bench, laughing into a chipped white mug with a cat on its side before she had finished her own joke, gone before he could hold her; here a night of terror in a city on fire; here the weight of a thing he had done and been ashamed of; here a grave. Grief after grief, guilt after guilt, drawn out and laid aside, so gently that the man on the couch smiled in his sleep. And what was left behind, banked and tended like coals, was the wanting. The wanting was never touched. Every time, the wanting was left alone.
The hall turned, or he turned in it, and he saw the thread.

It rose from the coin at his own temple, very fine, almost beautiful, and went up and away from him farther than he could follow. The white light let him feel what it carried. It carried him: a bishop wanting to be loved by his congregation; wanting to be asked for by name, and the count he kept and pretended not to keep; wanting the good chair beside Aurelian’s, and the Hierarch’s hand on his arm, and the peace that came at the Pearl; wanting a tidy answer, and then the next one, and the next. He had knelt every night of his life with nothing in his hands, and it had gone up out of him anyway, every hour of four hundred years, and he had never once felt it go. It went toward Sion. He could not see what was at the far end of it, and he was grateful that he could not.
He saw the dying go up.

He saw a man killed in a refinery fire on Titan, and a woman fallen from a gantry, and a child, a child, and he saw them rise through the Pearls of their homes into the City of the Throne, which was every bit as beautiful as he had told the grieving it would be. And it did not end for them. That was what he saw. The wanting went up with them and was kept, and fed, and made to want more, and it would not stop, not in a thousand years, not ever, because nothing there was ever finished, and nothing there was ever enough. Life without end, he had told their families. Life without end. He had said it over a thousand biers. He had meant it as a blessing.
And then he saw Mercy Hall.

He saw the white rooms he had walked through on Serenity, and the wardens moving through them with their calm, glad faces, the warm cups and the songs and the hands held, and he saw the people they released. He saw all of them. It was not possible that he saw all of them, and he saw them: a line of men and women and some who were barely more than children, standing quietly one behind another in the white light, a line that went back further than he could see, and every one of them had come there under the same words. They were written in light over each of them. Received into Mercy by the hand of Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life. He had signed them with a thought. He had signed them so easily. He had always asked that they be handled gently.

They stood before the City. He knew its wall, the jasper and the gold, and the gate that was a single pearl, and its light lay on the faces at the front of the line. And the gate did not open. He had watched it open more than thirty thousand times, for every soul he had ever sent up from a bier. It did not open for these. No clerk lifted a hand. No one said Received. They stood in the light outside it, patient, and one by one, as he watched, they went out, the way lamps go out along a street in the morning: not taken up, not taken in, not taken anywhere. The City did not so much as turn its face. Over each place where one of them had stood the word hung a moment longer in the air, Released, and then it went too.

He understood then what Mercy Hall was. The door at the back of the white room opened on reclamation and on nothing else. No one was resting. Every soft light in every alcove on every world, where a family laid a place each evening for someone who was being healed, was lit for no one at all, and he had blessed them. He had sent Stephen there. He had signed the form himself, believing he was opening a door.
Only the white light did not go out. It stood where they had stood, as if it had lost nothing.
He began to count them, and could not stop counting, and could not reach the end.

The worst of it was their faces. There was no accusation in them. They looked at him patiently, almost with pity, as at a man who had not yet understood something. And at the very end of the line, white-haired and bent, with a cloth bag held against his chest, there was the old man from the market, looking at him exactly as he had looked at him over the spilled saffron, as if he were remembering him.
Sol tried to say his name. He tried to say Stephen, and nothing came.
Then all of it fell away, the hall and the colonies and the City and the line of faces, and there was only the light.

It was not outside him now; it was through him, the way sun goes through a hand held up against it, and everything he had kept hidden from himself for so long was lit and seen and known. It should have been unbearable. It was unbearable. And at the center of it, holding him there, was something he could only have called kindness, if kindness could burn.
A voice spoke. It was not loud. It said his name the way the old man had said it, the way no one living said it, as if they were friends.
“Sol. Sol, why do you hunt me?”

He did not understand. He had never hunted anyone. He had only signed, and blessed, and believed, and asked that they be handled gently. And even as he thought it, he saw the line of faces again in his mind, and knew.
“Who are you?” he said. He did not know if he had a mouth to say it with. “Who are you?”
“Seek Christ,” the voice said, “and you will find me.”

He had heard it before. He had heard it twice in a room under the ice of Serenity, and once more in a white room at the bottom of it, in a dying man’s mouth, and every time it had slid out of him like water through his fingers before he could close them on it. He had never kept it long enough to hear it as a name. Now it went into him the way the light had gone into him, all the way through, and stayed.
Then the light grew brighter still, so bright that there was nothing else in it, not even him, and it poured into his eyes like water into a cup, and filled them, and overflowed.
When he came back, it was dark.

He did not know where he was. He did not know, for a while, who he was. There was a floor under his cheek, cool and faintly ridged, and his whole body ached. His tongue was thick and sore and tasted of copper. His head pounded. Someone was holding his shoulder and saying a word over and over, and it took him a long time to understand that the word was meant for him.
“Your Grace. Your Grace. Can you hear me?”
Pell. The name came up slowly, like something lifted from deep water. Deacon Pell.
“I can hear you.” His voice came out slurred and strange. He tried again. “Turn on the lights.”
There was a silence.
“Your Grace,” Pell said, very carefully, “they’re on.”

Sol lay still. He opened his eyes as wide as they would go. He could feel the air on them. There was nothing. Not darkness, quite, because darkness had depth and this did not; it was like a wall set against his face. Somewhere beyond it Jupiter was filling the long port, and he could not see it, and he could not see Pell, and he could not see his own hand when he lifted it to touch his eyes.
Another voice spoke, higher, further off. The steward. “Sir. Deacon. I have to call it in. It’s procedure. I saw...”
“His Grace fainted,” Pell said. “He’s overdue for Renewal. It’s the Renewal sickness. It happens.”
“That wasn’t fainting.” The young man’s voice shook. “I saw it. I know what it looks like. My whole section did the training. He went stiff, and he cried out, and he fell, and then he...”
“You’re mistaken,” Pell said quietly.
“Deacon, he was talking after. You heard him. You heard what he said.”
“His Grace said nothing,” Pell said. “He was confused. He’s very tired. We’ll be in Concord in nine hours, and I will see to him, and you will bring us two more cups of water. Thank you.”
There was a long pause. Then footsteps, going away.
Sol found Pell’s sleeve and held it. His fingers were weak. “What did I say?”
“Nothing, Your Grace.”
He had known Pell for sixty years. He had never once heard him lie. He had not known, until that moment, that he would recognize it when he did.

They got him back into the seat. He remembered little of the rest of the crossing. He slept, heavily, and woke aching with his eyes open on nothing, and slept again. Once he heard Pell murmuring into his Halo, arranging things: a closed car, the side entrance of the residence, no visitors. And once, close above him, Pell said in a voice of mild surprise that the Renewal office at Concord had written. There had been an opening at the chapel there, four days from now, at the morning office, and they had moved him up from the autumn. “I didn’t ask them, Your Grace,” Pell said. “It was simply there.” Sol heard it, and was too tired to wonder at it, and slept. Once he felt the cup pressed into his hands and drank, and his bitten tongue stung, and he thought of a thread of blood running out of an old man’s mouth onto Martian tiles, and of a small soft light above a bed under the ice, lit for no one.

At Concord Pell put a hood over his head and led him by the arm. Ganymede’s pull was faint and familiar under his feet, and the concourse was a roar of sound with nothing in it. Twice someone said “Remember the Mountain, Your Grace,” warmly, close by, and he turned his blind face toward the voice and could not answer, and Pell answered for him.
At the residence he felt stone steps, and then carpet, and then the edge of his own bed against his knees, and he sat down on it, and the strength went out of him all at once.
“I’ll tell the staff you’re ill,” Pell said. “Renewal sickness. You’ll see no one. It’s four days to the Renewal; it will put everything right.”
“My case.”
“Your Grace?”
“Bring me my case. Then leave me.”
Pell brought it. Sol heard him set it at the foot of the bed, and stand there a moment, and go. The door closed.

He found the clasps by touch. He set the vestments and the Book of Life aside on the floor without caring where they fell. Underneath, wrapped in the shirt, he found the other two. One was soft and crumbling at the edges, and when his fingers pressed it, something came away from it like dry leaves. The other was firmer, a notebook, its pages stiff with handwriting he could not see.
He lay back on the bed with both of them against his chest, as the old man had held them in the market, and stared up into nothing.

The word was still in him. He did not say it. He held it in his mouth the way the ancients, he had read once, put a coin under the tongues of their dead, and he did not say it, and he did not let it go.
